bib.title: Bandit Algorithms, Chapter 14: Foundations of Information Theory

question: What information-theoretic tools (entropy, relative entropy, Bretagnolle-Huber, Pinsker) are needed to make bandit lower-bound arguments rigorous?
contributions: Defines entropy and relative entropy via optimal coding, and extends relative entropy to general measurable spaces by discretisation (Eq. 14.5, Thm 14.1)
States and proves the Bretagnolle-Huber inequality (Thm 14.2) and applies it to Gaussian hypothesis testing
Notes on tightening (14.11), Pinsker (14.12), Hellinger and chi-squared distances (14.16)

results.claim: Relative entropy is not a distance: it is neither symmetric nor satisfies the triangle inequality.

results.claim: Bretagnolle-Huber: P(A)+Q(A^c) >= (1/2) exp(-D(P,Q)) for every event A.

results.claim: Single-observation Gaussian test between means 0 and Delta with SNR Delta^2/sigma^2 <= 1: some error probability is at least 3/20 under either hypothesis.
results.setup: X ~ N(mu, sigma^2), mu in {0, Delta}, one observation, any decision rule A

results.claim: Bretagnolle-Huber is proved through the stronger bound int min(p,q) >= (1/2) exp(-D), using Le Cam's inequality, Cauchy-Schwarz and Jensen.
Pinsker: total variation delta(P,Q) <= sqrt(D(P,Q)/2), giving P(A)+Q(A^c) >= 1 - sqrt(D/2); better than Thm 14.2 when D is small, worse when D is large.

results.claim: Chain of divergences: TV^2 <= Hellinger^2 <= D(P,Q) <= chi^2(P,Q); each tight alone but not jointly.
results.setup: Cites Tsybakov 2008 ch. 2; chi^2 needs P << Q

limits: Pure foundations chapter: no experiments, no numbers beyond the constants in worked examples.
Divergence decomposition (chain rule, Eq. 14.17) is only an exercise with a hint; the bandit-specific form is in later chapters, not here.
Entropy-coding intuition only for countable alphabets; general case is by discretisation.
Says nothing on RLHF, KL penalties, forward vs reverse KL, or estimating KL by sampling.
practices: Use base-2 logs for coding intuition but the natural log (nats) elsewhere (sec 14.1).
Apply Bretagnolle-Huber with whichever of D(P,Q) or D(Q,P) is smaller (sec 14.2).
Prefer Pinsker when D(P,Q) is small and Bretagnolle-Huber when it is large (Note 5, Fig 14.2).

terms.definition: H(P) = sum over p_i>0 of p_i log(1/p_i); nats for natural log, bits for base 2
D(P,Q) = sum p_i log(p_i/q_i); general case = int log(dP/dQ) dP if P << Q, else infinity
